title: Analytics Workflow Knowledge Base
lede: Modeling is only step three of the workflow. Whether an analysis creates value depends on whether the problem was framed correctly, whether the data can be trusted, and whether the results actually change a decision. The four stages below unfold in sequence and then loop back to the start.
principles: At every step, ask: which decision will this change? If you can't say, don't go any further yet.
Everything in code and under version control; every number can be traced back to its source and calculation logic.
Be explicit about intervals, assumptions and limitations; decision-makers need to know the worst case, not just a point estimate.
loop: Post-launch monitoring results, new findings and failure cases are the inputs to the next round of problem framing. Analytics is a loop, not a straight line.

stages.name: Problem Framing
stages.q: Whose decision will the results of this analysis change, and which one?
stages.summary: The most common reason analyses fail is not that the model isn't good enough, but that the problem was framed wrong. This step turns a vague business concern into a concrete question that data can answer and whose answer will shape a decision.

compares.title: Problem-driven vs. Data-driven
rows: Starting point
A business question or decision: "Why did the Q3 renewal rate drop?"
A dataset: "We have app event logs; let's see what we can find."
Process
Question → hypothesis → data needed → analysis → confirm or reject the hypothesis
Data → exploration → patterns → hypotheses → search for use cases
Best suited for
Clear objective, decision deadline, known stakeholders
New data sources or new markets where the problem space hasn't taken shape
Strengths
Focused and efficient; results map directly to action
Can surface opportunities nobody anticipated; fewer preconceptions
Risks
Confirmation bias: looking only for evidence that supports the hypothesis; framing the problem too narrowly
Fishing: run enough tests and something will always be "significant"; findings that nobody uses
Output
Recommendations for a specific decision
A list of new hypotheses and questions
compares.verdict: Lead with problem-driven work and use data-driven work to supplement it. Use data-driven exploration to generate hypotheses, then return to the problem-driven workflow to test them. The criterion fits in one sentence: if you can't say which decision the result will change, you're not ready to start the analysis.

sections.title: SCQA: Frame the Problem in Four Sentences
sections.body: Situation (facts everyone agrees on) → Complication (what has changed) → Question (what therefore needs answering) → Answer (the current most likely answer, as a hypothesis, and the recommended direction). Before the analysis, A is an initial hypothesis to be tested; afterward, it is replaced by an evidence-backed conclusion. If you can't write these four sentences, the problem hasn't been thought through yet.
sections.example:
S: Subscription revenue has grown steadily over the past two years.
C: The Q3 renewal rate fell from 82% to 76%.
Q: What is the main driver of the decline, and which issue should we tackle first?
A (initial hypothesis): The main driver is churn on the SMB plan after the Q3 price change; test price sensitivity first and, if confirmed, prioritize launching an SMB renewal offer.

sections.title: Issue Trees and Hypothesis Trees (MECE)
sections.body: Break the core question into mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive sub-questions, each mapped to a testable hypothesis and the data it requires. That is the essence of a problem-driven approach: hypothesis first, then decide which data to look at.
items: Issue tree: question → sub-questions; used to diagnose "where the problem lies"
Hypothesis tree: answer → supporting arguments; used to verify "whether it is true"
Tag each branch with its validation method, required data and owner

sections.title: Driver Tree
sections.body: Decompose the target metric into multiplicative or additive drivers to pinpoint where the problem sits, and to show each team which lever it owns.
sections.example:
Revenue = Traffic × Conversion rate × Average order value
Conversion rate = Add-to-cart rate × Checkout completion rate

sections.title: Identify the Question Type
sections.body: The question type determines which methods to use in step 03. Ask about the same topic in a different way and you get an entirely different analysis.
items: Descriptive: What happened? (Revenue by region last quarter)
Inferential: Is this difference real? What is it associated with?
Causal: How much impact did this change have?
Predictive: What happens next? Who will churn?
Prescriptive: What should we do, and for whom?

sections.title: Decision-first
sections.body: Before the analysis starts, write down who makes the decision, what the options are, and which result leads to which option. Set thresholds in advance to avoid finishing only to find the result is "interesting, but doesn't change anything," and to avoid post-hoc rationalization.
items: Effect > 2%: full rollout
Effect within ±1%: keep the status quo and save the development cost
Negative effect: stop and investigate why

sections.title: Success Metrics and Guardrail Metrics
sections.body: Success metrics measure the goal you are trying to improve; guardrail metrics ensure nothing else important is sacrificed.
items: Success metrics: directly tied to the decision, sensitive enough, measurable within a reasonable time frame
Guardrail metrics: metrics that must not get worse, such as revenue, latency, complaints and cancellation rate
Avoid vanity metrics: they only go up and are unrelated to value (e.g., cumulative sign-ups)

checklist: The question to be answered can be stated in one sentence
It is clear who will use the results and what decision they will make
Key hypotheses and how to test them are listed
Success metrics, guardrail metrics and decision thresholds are defined
Timeline, data availability and scope (what's in, what's out) are confirmed
pitfalls: Solving the wrong problem
Taking the request literally ("build me a churn model") without asking about the decision behind it; the real question is "who should get the retention budget," which is a causal/uplift problem.
Misaligned metrics
The team optimizes click-through rate while the company cares about long-term retention.
Scope creep
Without a clear scope, the analysis keeps growing and never gets finished.
Post-hoc storytelling
Looking at the data first, then picking the slices that support the conclusion (HARKing).
deliverables: One-page problem statement: background (SCQA), core question, hypotheses, decision and thresholds, metrics, scope, timeline

links.label: Power analysis: how much data you need
Uplift: the right way to ask "whom should we target"

stages.name: Data & Quality
stages.q: Can this data be trusted? Are the definitions consistent? Is it reproducible?
stages.summary: Garbage in, garbage out. Data architecture determines whether metric definitions stay consistent and whether analyses are reproducible; data quality determines whether conclusions can be trusted. The output of this step is a trustworthy, reproducible analytical dataset with consistent definitions.

layers.name: Raw layer
layers.desc: Stores source data untouched, with only minimal processing (formats, timestamps). Traceable and re-runnable.

layers.name: Integration layer
layers.desc: Cleans, deduplicates and standardizes definitions and dimensions, integrating data into subject-area detail and summary tables. Define once, share across the company.

layers.name: Application layer
layers.desc: Wide tables and metric tables serving specific reports, dashboards or model features.

layers.name: Application layer
layers.desc: Transforms raw data directly into reporting or analysis tables; logic is scattered across individual tables.

compares.title: Three-layer vs. Two-layer Architecture
rows: Layers
ODS → DWD/DWS → ADS; or Bronze → Silver → Gold (Medallion)
Raw/Staging → Mart
Metric definitions
Defined once in the integration layer; consistent company-wide
Each application transforms the data its own way, often producing "one metric, three numbers"
Reusability
High: subject-area tables in the integration layer can be shared by multiple applications
Low: logic is scattered across application tables, and work gets duplicated
Development speed
Slow up front; requires modeling and governance first
Fast; well suited to quick validation
Cost of change
Source changes only require updating the integration layer; downstream is unaffected
Source changes affect every table that depends on it directly
Best suited for
Multiple teams and product lines that need a single source of truth
Small teams, a single product, early exploration or POCs
compares.verdict: With few use cases and a small team, two layers are enough; once "the same metric doesn't reconcile across departments," that is the signal to add an integration layer. The Kimball (dimensional modeling) vs. Inmon (enterprise data warehouse) debate is, at its core, also about where the integration layer sits and how to build it; the Medallion architecture (Bronze/Silver/Gold) common in cloud lakehouses is a three-layer architecture.

compares.title: ETL vs. ELT
rows: Process
Clean the data in a separate transformation environment, then load it into the warehouse
Load the data into the warehouse as-is, then transform it in the warehouse with SQL
Where transformation happens
Outside the warehouse (ETL tools, Spark jobs)
Inside the warehouse (using the cloud warehouse's compute)
Raw data
Usually not retained; discarded after transformation
Fully retained; can be re-transformed at any time
Flexibility
Changing requirements means changing the pipeline and re-extracting
Just edit the SQL model and re-run; analysts can contribute too
Cost structure
Transformation-environment costs; less warehouse storage
Warehouse compute and storage costs; query spend needs to be controlled
Privacy & compliance
PII can be masked before loading, so sensitive data never lands
Raw PII lands in the warehouse, requiring access controls and masking policies
Typical tools
Informatica, SSIS, Talend, in-house Spark
Fivetran/Airbyte + dbt + Snowflake/BigQuery/Databricks
compares.verdict: In the cloud era, ELT is the default: storage is cheap, warehouse compute is powerful, and keeping the raw data lets you redefine metrics later. ETL is still needed when PII must be masked before loading, when source volumes are large enough that they must be filtered first, or when streaming data must be processed first. In practice it is often a hybrid, EtLT: only lightweight masking and format conversion before loading, with the heavy business logic kept in the warehouse and handled in dbt.

quality.title: Six Dimensions of Data Quality
dims: Is all the expected data there?
Missing rate; row counts match the source system
Reconcile against source systems or financial figures
Is the same fact identical across tables?
Is the data available when it's needed?
Do the values conform to formats and business rules?

sections.title: Quality Assurance Mechanisms
sections.body: Quality can't depend on eyeballing the data; it depends on mechanisms.
items: Data contracts: upstream teams commit to fields, types, semantics and refresh times, and must give notice before any change
Automated tests: dbt tests (not_null, unique, relationships, accepted_values), Great Expectations
Data lineage: know which tables each metric is computed from, so you can assess the blast radius when something breaks upstream
Monitoring and alerting: track row counts, missing rates and distribution shift daily

sections.title: Unified Metric Definitions (Semantic Layer)
sections.body: Codify metric definitions (numerator, denominator, filters, time window) and manage them centrally, so every report and analysis references the same definition.
sections.example: Active users = accounts with at least one valid interaction in the past 28 days (excluding test accounts and bots)
items: Tools: dbt Semantic Layer, LookML, Cube

sections.title: Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)
sections.body: Understand the data before modeling. The goal is not pretty charts but finding the data issues that could affect the conclusions.
items: Univariate: distributions, missing values, outliers
Temporal: trends, seasonality, breaks (often caused by tracking or system changes)
Relationships: association with the target variable, collinearity
Segments: whether different groups behave differently (watch out for Simpson's paradox)

checklist: The definition, source and refresh frequency of every field are known
Reconciled against a trusted source (row counts, totals)
Duplicates, missing values and outliers handled, and the treatment documented
Time zones and cutoffs of time fields are consistent
Every feature is available at prediction time (no data leakage)
The data-processing pipeline can be re-run (in code, under version control)
pitfalls: Data leakage
Using information not yet available at prediction time (e.g., using "refunded or not" to predict "satisfied or not"): great offline, collapses in production.
Survivorship bias
Analyzing only the customers who stayed and ignoring those who have already churned.
Inconsistent definitions
Two reports define "active users" differently, and meetings are spent reconciling numbers.
Tracking changes
A new version of the tracking code breaks a metric's continuity, and the break is mistaken for a business change.
Not reproducible
Data cleaned by hand in a notebook; three months later, nobody knows where the numbers came from.
deliverables: Data dictionary (field definitions, sources, metric definitions)
Data quality report (check results across the six dimensions)
Re-runnable data-processing code and the analytical dataset

links.label: Anomaly detection: automatically flag suspicious data
KS test: check whether two distributions differ

stages.name: Modeling & Analysis
stages.q: Which method answers the question? How far can the results be trusted?
stages.summary: The question type determines the method, not the latest model. Identify the question type first, pick the corresponding method family, and use the simplest possible baseline to confirm that a complex model is really worth it.

routing.title: Question Type → Method Family

rows.q: What happened? What was revenue by region last quarter?
Is the difference between the two groups real? Which factors are associated with churn?
How much impact did this change have?
Who will churn? What will demand be next month?
Who should get a discount? Which version should we ship?

routing.note: Prediction ≠ causation. A churn model tells you "who will leave," not "who will stay because of a retention effort." "What to do, and for whom" is a causal question.

sections.title: Start with a Baseline
sections.body: Every complex model must first beat a simple baseline: the historical average, the last period's value, a business rule, a logistic regression. If it can't beat the baseline, there is no case for deploying a complex model; the margin by which it wins is the value of the added complexity.

sections.title: Design Validation to Mirror Production
sections.body: The purpose of validation is to estimate "post-launch performance," so the split must match how the model will actually be used.
items: Time-based split: train on the past, validate on the future (the right choice for most business problems)
Group split: the same customer must never appear in both the training and validation sets
Keep a test set that has never been looked at; don't tune repeatedly on the validation set

sections.title: Align Evaluation Metrics with Business Costs
sections.body: Metrics should reflect the real cost of errors.
items: Imbalanced classification: look at PR-AUC and Recall@K, not accuracy
Ordinal grading: QWK heavily penalizes errors that are "many grades off" (e.g., insurance underwriting tiers)
Decision threshold: set it based on misclassification costs, not the default 0.5
Demand forecasting: provide P10/P50/P90 so decision-makers can see the risk

sections.title: Explainable ≠ Causal
sections.body: SHAP and feature importance describe "how the model uses this variable"; they do not mean "changing this variable will change the outcome." To answer the latter, you have to go back to causal inference methods.

sections.title: Quantify Uncertainty
sections.body: Every number should come with its uncertainty: a confidence interval, a prediction interval or a bootstrap distribution.
items: Estimates: confidence intervals or credible intervals
Predictions: prediction intervals (wider than confidence intervals)
When no formula is available: bootstrap

sections.title: Robustness Checks
sections.body: A conclusion shouldn't hold only under one particular configuration.
items: Does the conclusion change under a different, reasonable set of assumptions or parameters?
Subgroup analysis: does the conclusion hold only for one group? (Remember to correct for multiple comparisons.)
Causal analysis: placebo tests, sensitivity analysis for unmeasured confounding

checklist: The method matches the question type (descriptive / inferential / causal / predictive / prescriptive)
A simple baseline exists, and the complex model's lift over it is quantified
The validation split mirrors real production conditions
Evaluation metrics reflect business costs
Results come with quantified uncertainty
Robustness checks are done
pitfalls: Answering causal questions with predictive models
Reading feature importance as "improve this factor and the outcome will improve."
Overfitting the validation set
Tuning repeatedly on the same validation set, then seeing a large performance gap after launch.
Multiple comparisons
Slice the data into 20 subgroups and one will always come out "significant."
Reporting only the average
The average effect is positive, but it is negative for some key customer segments.
Complexity worship
Trading a 0.5% AUC gain for a model that is hard to maintain and hard to explain.
deliverables: Analysis or model report: methods, assumptions, results, uncertainty, limitations
Reproducible code and a model card

links.label: Bootstrap: intervals when there's no formula
BH correction: multiple comparisons in subgroup analysis
XGBoost: a strong baseline for tabular prediction

stages.name: Deployment & Value
stages.q: Did the results actually change a decision and create measurable value?
stages.summary: An analysis nobody uses might as well not have been done. Deployment comes down to three things: embedding the results in the decision process, validating the real impact with experiments, and monitoring continuously while feeding what you learn into the next round of problem framing.

compares.title: Batch vs. Real-time
rows: How outputs are produced
Computed on a schedule (daily, weekly), with results written to tables
Computed on the fly when a request comes in, and returned immediately
Latency
Hours to a day
Milliseconds to seconds
Architectural complexity
Low: scheduler + tables
High: API service, real-time features, latency and availability monitoring
Suited decisions
List-based: marketing lists, risk tiers, replenishment plans
Interactive: recommendations, fraud detection, dynamic pricing
Feature consistency
Training and inference share the same batch code, so consistency is easy
Online and offline features easily drift apart; often requires a feature store
Cost
Low
High (always-on services, ops headcount)
compares.verdict: If batch will do, don't go real-time. Ask first: does the decision really have to be made within seconds? Most business decisions (lists, tiers, budget allocation) are fine with a daily refresh; real-time is only worth its cost when a user's in-the-moment behavior changes the decision.

sections.title: Embed in the Decision Process
sections.body: Results must show up where decision-makers actually decide (CRM lists, fields in operational systems, daily reports), not in a slide deck.
items: Define explicitly: who takes which action, at what point, based on which output
Recommend actions, not just scores: "Contact these 500 first" beats "churn probability 0.73"
Design human review and exception-handling processes

sections.title: Validate the Real Impact
sections.body: Good offline metrics don't mean the business will improve. Treat the launch itself as an experiment.
items: Shadow mode: the new model scores but doesn't act; compare it against the current approach
Small-traffic A/B test: validate business metrics on 5–10% of traffic
Gradual ramp-up: roll out fully only after confirming guardrail metrics haven't deteriorated
Long-term holdout: keep measuring cumulative value

sections.title: Monitoring and Operations
sections.body: Once deployed, models quietly lose accuracy as the environment changes; monitoring is part of deployment.
items: Data monitoring: upstream fields, row counts, missing rates
Drift monitoring: whether input distributions (PSI, KS test) and prediction distributions have shifted
Performance monitoring: track actual accuracy once ground-truth labels come in
Retraining triggers: on a fixed schedule, or when drift/performance crosses a threshold

sections.title: Communication: The Pyramid Principle
sections.body: Conclusion first: lead with the answer and the recommendation, then the supporting arguments, and only then the methods and details. What decision-makers want is "so what should we do."
sections.example:
Conclusion: Concentrate the retention budget on the 20% of customers with the highest uplift, retaining an estimated 1,200 more customers per quarter.
Supporting points: ① The experiment shows retention efforts are 3× as effective for this group as on average ② For the remaining 80%, the retention effect is close to 0 ③ The budget stays the same.
Limitations: The effect is estimated from the Q2 experiment and may differ in peak season.

sections.title: Measure ROI and Close the Loop
sections.body: Convert the effect into business value (revenue, cost, risk), and feed the new problems observed after launch back into the next round of problem framing.
items: Incremental value = effect measured in the experiment × scale − development and operating costs
Record every decision and its outcome to build up organizational learning

checklist: Who acts, when, on which output, and with what action is defined
Business impact is validated with an experiment or a control group
Monitoring and alerting cover data, drift and performance
Model versioning and a rollback mechanism are in place
Conclusions are communicated using the Pyramid Principle, with limitations stated
ROI is estimated and a review date is scheduled
pitfalls: Breaking the last mile
The model is built but never wired into any system or process.
Good offline, poor online
Features differ between training and serving, or there is data leakage.
No control group
Metrics rise after launch, but there is no way to tell whether the model or seasonality deserves the credit.
Model decay
The environment changes and the model quietly loses accuracy without anyone noticing.
Feedback-loop bias
The model only acts on high-scoring customers, so future training data contains only treated samples.
deliverables: Deployment plan (decision process, architecture, ramp-up plan)

links.label: A/B testing: validate the impact of a launch
Sequential testing: continuous monitoring during ramp-up
CausalImpact: when you can't run an experiment
